 Roxie Hammill 
 November 17, 2026 
 Elections 
 4 min. read 
 JoCo election chief drew criticism for closing early voting sites. She says they ‘worked perfectly’
 Turnout for the Nov. 3 election reached 63.5% in Johnson County, trailing only the 2020 and 2024 presidential elections, according to Election Commissioner Connie Schmidt. 
 Johnson County Election Commissioner Connie Schmidt speaks during the election canvass Nov. 16. Photo credit Beth Lipoff. 
 Two Johnson County officials had slightly different takes on the decision to close eight early voting sites, as final election results were certified Monday morning.
 Election Commissioner Connie Schmidt, who made the decision to close eight sites while opening two more, said about the choice, “The 12 [total early voting] locations worked perfectly. They served voters equally across the county.”
 The proof, she said, was in the all-time record of 8,185 ballots cast at the 12 voting locations between 8 a.m. and noon on the Monday before Election Day. Two years ago, only two advance voting sites were open that day and just 5,926 ballots were cast.
 Still, County Commission Chair Mike Kelly had reservations about the shuttered sites.
 “If we can find opportunities to make voting more convenient and available for students at the community college or for neighborhoods that may be more transportation-challenged, I think we should explore those opportunities,” he said on Monday.
 Schmidt’s decision over the summer reduced the total number of advance polling places from 18 to 12 and drew protests ahead of the August primary.
 Early voters cast their ballots on Tuesday, Oct. 20, at Hilltop Conference Center Blue Valley in Overland Park. Photo credit Kylie Graham. 
 Kelly, the ACLU and others said the eliminated sites were in potentially marginalized areas underserved by public transportation. A site at Johnson County Community College was one of those shut down.
 After the decision to shutter eight sites was made, Kelly wrote to Schmidt asking for the sites to be restored, and protesters took up the cause outside the election office.
 But after it was all said and done, Kelly praised the efforts of the county election team as the certification ended on Monday, citing their professionalism, courtesy and dedication. Still, he indicated he’d be open to more discussion about the early polling sites for future elections.
 “After any election is a great opportunity to get a pulse check with the community — how folks chose to vote and how we can continue to try to encourage as many people as possible to participate in the election process,” he said.
 County completed canvassing its election results
 Although the Johnson County Election Office receives county financial support, its decisions are independent from the county commission. Election commissioners in Johnson County are appointed by the Kansas Secretary of State.
 The meeting Monday between commission members, who also act as the county board of canvassers, set official election results for the county.
 On Friday, the board reviewed and approved which provisional ballots would be counted. The official total announced Monday folded in those provisional ballots to the total.
 The state board of canvassers now has until the first business day of the month after the election to certify at the state level.
 A historic non-presidential year turnout
 Total Johnson County turnout for the Nov. 3 midterm was 63.5%, with 303,407 total ballots cast.
 That was historically high turnout for a year with no presidential election, tracking just behind the 2020 and 2024 presidential years, Schmidt said.
 A majority of voters voted early, with 54% casting advance ballots in person. Another 35% voted on Election Day itself and 10.5% voted by mail.
 A sign for voters is posted up at the Johnson County Arts & Heritage Center on Election Day. Photo credit Kylie Graham. 
 For mail-in ballots, there was an 88% return rate, with the majority of those returned — about 80% — coming back to the election office via 16 drop boxes rather than the Postal Service, Schmidt said.
 With delivery delays in the postal service a continuing issue, Schmidt has emphasized the drop boxes as a way to ensure ballots make it to the election office in time. That may become more important in future elections because state legislators have voted to end the three-day grace period for ballots that have been postmarked by Election Day.
 This November, 61 ballots were received after the three-day grace period and could not be counted.
 Close races
 Johnson County election workers had an extra load this fall because of the state-required audit of three close statewide races and two state House races . An audit is required by state law when a race is within 1% after election night.
 It required hand-counting of ballots from 10% of precincts that voted in a race. That extra work this year resulted in a cost of more than $80,000 to the county.
 Two Kansas House races remained close on Monday.
 From left, Democrat Sara Kiewiet and Republican Rep. Sean Tarwater. File photos. 
 House District 27 , which is entirely within Johnson County in southern Leawood and Overland Park, still showed Democrat Sara Kiewiet ahead of Republican incumbent Rep. Sean Tarwater, now by 84 votes, with 6,997 votes for Kiewiet and 6,913 votes for Tarwater.
 In House District 117, which is made up of parts of Johnson and Douglas counties, the Secretary of State’s office showed Democrat Brandon Holland ahead of Republican incumbent Adam Turk, 6,611 votes to 6,469. However, the count won’t be final until certified by the Secretary of State.
 Other odds and ends
 Commissioners resolved one tie with a coin toss on Monday.
 The tie between Jeff Huff and Jim Ferri, both write-ins for Olathe Township Clerk, was won by Ferri by a flip of a coin.
 Kids had an activity to do while waiting for their parents at polling places. They got to vote on some fun things unrelated to politics.
 They voted art as their favorite subject, pancakes as their favorite breakfast and Shawnee Mission Park as their favorite park. No audits or recounts required.
